summary:
LunaSelect is an integrated software platform developed to support the scientific assessment and selection of potential lunar landing sites. It addresses the challenge of identifying suitable locations on the Moon by combining terrain analysis, environmental modelling, geospatial data processing, and interactive 3D visualization.

The software processes lunar Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and GeoTIFF datasets to evaluate terrain characteristics such as slope, roughness, elevation, surface relief, and potential crater hazards. It also integrates NASA Moon Trek for lunar imagery and JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth ephemeris data, supporting the assessment of illumination and Earth visibility.

LunaSelect provides automated data ingestion, validation, terrain visualization, preliminary suitability assessments, and downloadable scientific reports. Its modular architecture supports reproducible analysis while identifying uncertainties and missing information.

This project is important because lunar landing-site evaluation requires combining complex datasets and understanding multiple environmental risks. LunaSelect aims to make these analyses more accessible, transparent, and efficient, helping researchers and mission planners investigate candidate sites and make better-informed decisions.

Ultimately, LunaSelect transforms raw lunar data into actionable scientific insights for future lunar exploration
details:
LunaSelect: An Integrated Lunar Landing-Site Assessment and Decision-Support Platform

1. PROJECT OVERVIEW

LunaSelect is an independent, Python-based scientific software platform developed to analyze lunar surface conditions and support the identification of potentially suitable landing sites for future Moon exploration missions.

Selecting a lunar landing site is a complex scientific and engineering challenge. Mission planners must evaluate several interconnected factors, including terrain slope, surface roughness, crater distribution, solar illumination, Earth visibility, environmental conditions, scientific objectives, and uncertainty in available observations.

These factors are often represented by separate datasets with different resolutions, coordinate reference systems, measurement units, spatial coverage, and levels of scientific reliability.

LunaSelect addresses this challenge by integrating geospatial data processing, numerical terrain analysis, environmental modelling, astronomical data retrieval, preliminary suitability evaluation, and interactive three-dimensional visualization into a single research application.

The central objective of LunaSelect is to transform raw lunar datasets into understandable scientific information that supports systematic, transparent, and reproducible investigations of potential landing locations.

2. HOW DOES LUNASELECT WORK?

LunaSelect follows a structured workflow that begins with data ingestion and concludes with scientific visualization and preliminary assessment.

First, users upload lunar Digital Elevation Models, GeoTIFF rasters, or other supported datasets through an interactive graphical interface.

The software examines the dataset's dimensions, pixel resolution, coordinate reference system, NoData values, geographical coverage, metadata, and available provenance information.

After validation, an appropriate elevation model can be selected for terrain processing.

The terrain engine calculates elevation gradients, slope, aspect, surface roughness, local relief, curvature, and hillshade. It also contains an exploratory crater-candidate detection algorithm.

LunaSelect integrates JPL Horizons to retrieve astronomical information concerning the Sun, Earth, and Moon. This information supports investigations of solar illumination and Earth visibility.

The software also connects to NASA Moon Trek, allowing users to discover lunar imagery layers and preview available map tiles.

The application organizes the available information through analysis modules and provides interactive terrain visualizations, preliminary evaluation results, and scientific reports.

LunaSelect supports outputs in formats including PDF, JSON, CSV, OBJ, PLY, and GLB.

3. TERRAIN ANALYSIS AND SCIENTIFIC CAPABILITIES

Terrain characteristics are important because the physical structure of the lunar surface can influence landing feasibility, surface mobility, and operational planning.

LunaSelect includes several terrain-analysis functions.

Slope analysis determines the inclination of the lunar surface using elevation gradients. It helps researchers identify potentially steep or uneven regions.

Aspect analysis calculates the direction of steepest descent and provides information about the orientation of terrain surfaces.

Surface roughness analysis evaluates variations in elevation within a specified spatial window. This helps characterize terrain irregularities.

Local relief analysis measures elevation differences within surrounding areas and identifies regions with substantial topographic variation.

Curvature analysis evaluates changes in the shape of the surface and helps describe ridges, depressions, and other terrain features.

Hillshade analysis generates shaded terrain representations that improve the visual interpretation of topography.

Crater-candidate detection uses numerical image-processing methods to identify possible crater-like depressions. These detections are preliminary and require verification against suitable reference observations.

The platform also supports three-dimensional terrain reconstruction, allowing users to explore lunar surface geometry interactively.

Together, these functions help transform numerical elevation datasets into useful terrain maps and visual representations.

4. NASA JPL HORIZONS INTEGRATION

LunaSelect integrates the publicly available NASA JPL Horizons API to retrieve astronomical ephemeris information.

The Horizons system provides position and velocity information for Solar System bodies across specified time intervals.

The software can request Sun and Earth ephemerides relative to the Moon, supporting investigations of lunar environmental geometry.

For example, during development, LunaSelect successfully retrieved Earth position and velocity vectors relative to the Moon for multiple observation times.

The platform includes functions for calculating solar and terrestrial viewing directions and investigating possible terrain obstruction.

These capabilities are relevant to solar-power planning, illumination investigations, and direct Earth communications.

However, Horizons vectors must be transformed into the appropriate lunar coordinate system before they can be used as site-specific local viewing directions.

Accurate illumination-duration predictions also require appropriate terrain-horizon modelling, temporal sampling, and scientific validation.

Therefore, LunaSelect distinguishes preliminary environmental calculations from fully validated mission predictions.

5. NASA MOON TREK INTEGRATION

LunaSelect connects to NASA Moon Trek through its Web Map Tile Service.

Moon Trek provides access to lunar imagery products that can support surface visualization and geographic investigations.

The software can retrieve service information, discover available imagery layers, identify supported zoom levels, and request individual map tiles.

An additional DEM locator component examines an uploaded elevation model's geographic bounds and calculates candidate Moon Trek tile coordinates.

This helps researchers investigate whether relevant imagery may be available for their selected region.

During development, LunaSelect successfully retrieved Moon Trek service metadata and identified a lunar south-polar illumination product.

Some requested higher-resolution imagery tiles were unavailable. The software therefore distinguishes valid tile coordinates from confirmed imagery availability.

This is important because the absence of a requested imagery tile should not automatically be interpreted as a lack of sunlight or an unsuitable landing location.

6. THREE-DIMENSIONAL LUNAR TERRAIN VISUALIZATION

One of LunaSelect's important features is its ability to reconstruct lunar terrain using Digital Elevation Models.

The program converts elevation information into three-dimensional geometric structures consisting of vertices and surfaces.

These models help users understand the spatial relationships between elevated regions, depressions, ridges, and other terrain features.

Three-dimensional visualization can reveal topographic characteristics that are difficult to interpret from tables or two-dimensional images alone.

The software supports interactive previews and exports terrain meshes in OBJ, PLY, and GLB formats.

For large datasets, reduced-resolution previews are available to improve computational efficiency.

During development, LunaSelect successfully generated a three-dimensional terrain model from a real lunar elevation raster belonging to the A310 study region.

This demonstrates the software's ability to transform actual lunar geospatial data into an interactive research visualization.

7. REAL-DATA TESTING AND DEMONSTRATION

LunaSelect was tested using real lunar datasets associated with the A310 research region.

One of the principal datasets was A310_GLDELEV_005.tif.

The raster contained 3,200 rows and 3,200 columns, representing approximately 10.24 million elevation samples.

Its horizontal pixel spacing was 5 metres, covering an area of approximately 16 kilometres by 16 kilometres.

The dataset used a lunar south-polar stereographic coordinate reference system with a reference radius of 1,737,400 metres.

The reported minimum raster value was approximately 2,796.14, while the maximum was approximately 6,464.39.

The raster contained 100 percent valid pixels according to the performed masking check.

LunaSelect successfully read this file, preserved its numerical values, and generated a three-dimensional terrain model.

Additional validation compared LunaSelect's NoData masking with Rasterio, confirming matching invalid-pixel masks for a tested lunar image product.

The software's existing automated testing suite also passed 43 tests during development.

These results demonstrate the functionality of important processing components. However, the elevation product's vertical units were not explicitly declared in the examined metadata, and full scientific validation remains necessary before interpreting all derived measurements as physically calibrated results.

8. BENEFITS OF LUNASELECT

LunaSelect provides several benefits for lunar research and preliminary mission planning.

The first benefit is accessibility. The application organizes complex scientific procedures within an interactive interface, reducing the need for users to develop separate processing programs for every analytical task.

The second benefit is efficiency. Terrain processing, astronomical data retrieval, geospatial validation, visualization, and reporting can be performed within a unified software environment.

The third benefit is transparency. The platform preserves original datasets and records relevant processing information, allowing users to examine the sources and assumptions behind their assessments.

The fourth benefit is reproducibility. Structured configurations, dataset identifiers, and reporting functions help researchers repeat analyses and compare results.

The fifth benefit is visualization. Interactive maps and three-dimensional models improve the interpretation of complex lunar terrain.

The sixth benefit is expandability. LunaSelect's modular architecture allows additional scientific datasets, processing methods, and assessment criteria to be incorporated into future versions.

These benefits make the software potentially useful for education, independent planetary research, and early-stage exploration studies.

9. INTENDED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT

The long-term objective of LunaSelect is to improve the accessibility and systematic organization of lunar landing-site research.

Future lunar exploration missions will require detailed assessments of terrain hazards, environmental constraints, communication opportunities, and scientific objectives.

LunaSelect aims to contribute to this process by providing an integrated research environment for examining candidate locations.

The project is particularly relevant to lunar polar research, where low solar elevation, permanent and temporary shadows, complex terrain, and communication geometry create significant analytical challenges.

Another intended impact is educational accessibility.

Students, universities, and independent researchers may not have access to expensive or highly specialized planetary analysis infrastructure.

LunaSelect aims to provide a flexible framework through which users can explore lunar datasets, learn numerical techniques, and investigate surface conditions using commonly available computing resources.

Ultimately, the project seeks to support more informed, transparent, and evidence-based preliminary assessments of lunar landing locations.

10. TOOLS, PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES, AND TECHNOLOGIES USED

LunaSelect was developed primarily using Python.

Python provides the foundation for scientific calculations, geospatial processing, astronomical-data integration, user-interface functionality, and automated testing.

NumPy was used for numerical arrays, elevation-grid calculations, statistical operations, and mathematical processing.

SciPy was used for scientific computing, numerical algorithms, filtering, and terrain-analysis operations.

Rasterio was used to inspect georeferenced raster datasets, interpret coordinate information, and validate GeoTIFF data.

The tiff file library was used to decode and process TIFF files.

Streamlit was used to develop the interactive graphical application interface.

Plotly and Matplotlib were used for scientific visualization, graphs, terrain maps, and three-dimensional previews.

ReportLab was used to generate PDF reports.

JSON, YAML, and CSV were used for project configurations, structured data storage, metadata, and scientific result exchange.

NASA JPL Horizons was integrated for astronomical ephemeris retrieval.

NASA Moon Trek was integrated for lunar imagery service discovery and tile previews.

Git and GitHub were used for source-code management and project sharing.

Python unittest and coverage tools were used for automated testing, regression checking, and examination of source-code execution.

The software was developed and tested in a Windows computing environment using Python virtual environments and PowerShell.

No specialized spacecraft hardware was required for its current data-processing and visualization functions.

11. WHAT MAKES LUNASELECT CREATIVE AND INNOVATIVE?

LunaSelect's principal innovation lies in combining several traditionally separate scientific workflows into one accessible platform.

Lunar landing-site analysis involves planetary science, mathematics, geographic information systems, astronomy, environmental modelling, computer programming, and engineering decision-making.

LunaSelect brings these disciplines together within a unified research environment.

Rather than requiring users to move repeatedly between multiple programs, the project aims to offer an integrated sequence from dataset ingestion to preliminary scientific assessment and visualization.

Another innovative element is the combination of real lunar elevation models with publicly available NASA data services.

The project integrates local numerical terrain analysis with astronomical ephemerides and external imagery discovery, allowing multiple sources of scientific information to be investigated together.

LunaSelect also emphasizes explainable preliminary assessment.

The software's evaluation architecture distinguishes safety constraints, weighted factors, uncertainty, and missing information.

This is important because incomplete data should not produce misleading conclusions about landing suitability.

The project is also designed to be modular, allowing the incorporation of new scientific models and additional planetary datasets.

Its creativity therefore comes from its integrated architecture, transparent scientific workflow, and focus on making advanced lunar analysis more accessible.

12. FACTORS CONSIDERED DURING DEVELOPMENT

The project was designed around the understanding that lunar landing-site suitability depends on multiple interconnected considerations.

Terrain slope was considered because steep surfaces can create landing and mobility challenges.

Surface roughness was included because irregular terrain can affect mechanical stability and surface operations.

Crater distribution was considered because craters and their surrounding terrain can introduce potential hazards.

Boulder hazards were recognized as important, although reliable identification of individual boulders requires sufficiently detailed observations.

Solar illumination was considered because sunlight influences the operation of solar-powered instruments and spacecraft systems.

Terrain shadowing was considered because nearby ridges, crater walls, and other elevated features can obstruct direct sunlight.

Earth visibility was included because direct Earth communication may depend on local viewing geometry.

Lunar geographic position and coordinate reference systems were considered to support accurate spatial interpretation.

Data resolution was considered because the reliability of hazard detection depends on the scale of the available observations.

Scientific uncertainty was considered because measurements, numerical approximations, and environmental models are never perfectly precise.

Dataset provenance and metadata were considered to ensure that users could examine where information originated.

Computational efficiency was considered because lunar DEMs may contain millions of pixels and require significant processing resources.

Mission-specific requirements were considered because different spacecraft and exploration objectives may demand different landing-site characteristics.

These factors shaped the software's analytical framework and development priorities.

13. CHALLENGES FACED DURING DEVELOPMENT

Several challenges were encountered while developing and testing LunaSelect.

One challenge involved reading large lunar GeoTIFF datasets with different compression methods and metadata structures.

Some files contained extreme negative NoData values, requiring careful interpretation to avoid including invalid pixels in scientific calculations.

Another challenge involved memory consumption and computational performance when processing large elevation grids.

Environmental calculations, especially terrain-shadow analysis across many pixels and observation times, can require substantial computational resources.

The project therefore incorporated reduced-resolution previews for exploratory analysis.

Geographic interoperability created additional challenges because external services and local DEM datasets did not always provide directly comparable coordinate reference information.

The Moon Trek integration demonstrated this issue when some calculated tile coordinates corresponded to unavailable imagery or uncertain geographic coverage.

Software integration also required extensive debugging, particularly when combining separately developed modules within the Streamlit interface.

Automated tests and independent mathematical checks helped identify functional and numerical issues.

These experiences reinforced the importance of reliable data validation, transparent limitations, reproducible testing, and modular software design.

14. FUTURE DEVELOPMENT AND IMPROVEMENTS

Future development will focus on improving automation, scientific accuracy, computational efficiency, and mission-specific analysis.

One priority is automatic identification and validation of uploaded scientific datasets.

Another priority is more comprehensive solar illumination modelling, including accurate coordinate transformations, terrain-horizon analysis, and longer observation intervals.

Higher-resolution surface-hazard analysis will also be important, particularly for reliable crater and boulder identification.

Improved geographic alignment between lunar datasets and external map services will enable more consistent integration of NASA imagery products.

The project also aims to expand uncertainty analysis, strengthen multi-site comparison, and improve the interpretation of missing or incomplete data.

Additional validation against independent numerical methods, real lunar observations, and annotated reference datasets will be necessary.

Performance optimization through caching, chunk-based processing, and improved computational algorithms will help the software handle larger research datasets.

The long-term goal is to develop LunaSelect into a more comprehensive and scientifically verified planetary surface assessment platform.

15. CONCLUSION

LunaSelect was developed to address the complexity of lunar landing-site assessment through an integrated, data-driven approach.

The software combines geospatial data processing, terrain analysis, astronomical information retrieval, environmental investigations, three-dimensional visualization, preliminary suitability evaluation, and scientific reporting.

The project has demonstrated successful processing of real lunar elevation datasets, generation of three-dimensional terrain models, retrieval of JPL Horizons ephemeris information, discovery of NASA Moon Trek imagery services, and automated verification of important software components.

Its primary contribution is an accessible framework that helps transform complex lunar datasets into structured and understandable scientific information.

By connecting numerical analysis, planetary science, and software engineering, LunaSelect aims to support future lunar research and improve the accessibility of early-stage mission assessment tools.

The project is designed to encourage more transparent, reproducible, and evidence-based investigations of lunar surface conditions.

Ultimately, LunaSelect demonstrates how integrated scientific software can contribute to a better understanding of the Moon and support informed planning for future exploration missions.
